So I have had this problem in my head for the last week and I havn't found a satisfying anwser yet.

Two partners are in a relationship. (lets call them John and Joan). On a scale both have an attractivness rating of 7 out of 10 points. This rating includes all traites that make you more attractive to the other sex (or the same sex in a gay relationship) . The rating thus includes intelligence, social stance, fame, looks, money etc.

Now the interesting part. Over night one John goes up on the scale to a 9, the other one stays at 7.

A. Would it be immoral for John who is now more attractive to find a new partner with a corresponding attractivness rating of 9?

Alternative scenario: Both Partners are a 7 on said scale. Overnight John drops in attractiveness to a 5.

B.Is Joan now obliged to stay with him?

I'd love to hear your take on the Problem!

On question A I thought that it wouldn't be immoral because he would just take the best thing he could get.

i'm not really sure though

No one is obligated to be in a relationship with anyone. If you are unhappy in your relationship and your partner isn't meeting your standards, you are free to leave the relationship. Staying with someone out of a sense of guilt won't do anyone any favors in the long run. It stings to get broken up with, sure, but most people bounce back and move on.

Obviously it gets more complicated if there are children involved or a lot of years invested in each other but just as a pure thought experiment based on the criteria you said, my take on it is that it isn't immoral to move from relationship to relationship trying to find the most happiness.

Sorry that I wasn't clear. My basic position is that it would not be wrong for either of them in either scenario to move on to another relationship.

Scenario B is probably a bit more justified, to the extent that you must justify your decision, in that it's kind of a bait-and-switch type situation.

One thing I'm curious is if your "attractive rating" includes the value of the history of a relationship.

Sure, it may be possible for a rating to change drastically (serious injury, acquired debt, etc., etc.) but the value of knowing someone and being part of their circle shouldn't be overlooked.
nice username, yss i would say it holds every value the other partner has

In my opinion that would be justified as they have no moral obligation to stay together, although if they have children they should be obliged to at the very least provide financial support to raise them. Being in a relationship you don't want to be in only hurts the relationship and generally causes more harm than leaving.

I would'nt say the person leaving (at least in scenario A) is a very [i]moral[/i] person, however, if they simply leave their partner as soon as they have the ability to get laid by someone wealthier and more attractive. They probably did not really love their partner in the first place, in which case it is probably better for their partner if they leave.

All of the things you listed (intelligence, social stance, fame, looks, money etc.) are of differing importance to everyone.

What you're really asking is:

If my partner isn't fulfilling my needs and I know I could find someone who will, is it immoral to leave them?

So I ask, what specific aspects are not enough for John in scenerio A? They are his subjective preferences; his pursuit of happiness. Same for Scenario B. We all seek our own happiness.

Mises Monday - 07-13-15 - Introduction Chapter 1 - Economics and Praxeology

Hello everyone, announcing a new feature here "Mises Monday" where we are going to read Ludwig von Mises' magnum opus in tiny bite size pieces every monday here on /v/libertarian. We are starting with the first introduction chapter entitled "Economics and Praxeology" in which Mises introduces the concept that economics and philosophy are intertwined due to the titular phrase "Human Action". Feel free to debate, discuss, read along, or don't, you know the drill.

  1. Economics and Praxeology Economics is the youngest of all sciences. In the last two hundred years, it is true, many new sciences have emerged from the disciplines familiar to the ancient Greeks. However, what happened here was merely that parts of knowledge which had already found their place in the complex of the old system of learning now became autonomous. The field of study was more nicely subdivided and treated with new methods; hitherto unnoticed provinces were discovered in it, and people began to see things from aspects different from those of their precursors. The field itself was not expanded. But economics opened to human science a domain previously inaccessible and never thought of. The discovery of a regularity in the sequence and interdependence of market phenomena went beyond the limits of the traditional system of learning. It conveyed knowledge which could be regarded neither as logic, mathematics, psychology, physics, nor biology.

Philosophers had long since been eager to ascertain the ends which God or Nature was trying to realize in the course of human history. They searched for the law of mankind's destiny and evolution. But even those thinkers whose inquiry was free from any theological tendency failed utterly in these endeavors because they were committed to a faulty method. They dealt with humanity as a whole or with other holistic concepts like nation, race, or church. They set up quite arbitrarily the ends to which the behavior of such wholes is bound to lead. But they could not satisfactorily answer the question regarding what factors compelled the various acting individuals to behave in such a way that the goal aimed at by the whole's inexorable evolution was attained. They had recourse to desperate shifts: miraculous interference of the Deity either by revelation or by the delegation of God-sent prophets and consecrated leaders, preestablished harmony, predestination, or the operation of a mystic and fabulous "world soul" or "national soul." Others spoke of a "cunning of nature" which implanted in man impulses driving him unwittingly along precisely the path Nature wanted him to take. [p. 2]

Other philosophers were more realistic. They did not try to guess the designs of Nature or God. They looked at human things from the viewpoint of government. They were intent upon establishing rules of political action, a technique, as it were, of government and statesmanship. Speculative minds drew ambitious plans for a thorough reform and reconstruction of society. The more modest were satisfied with a collection and systematization of the data of historical experience. But all were fully convinced that there was in the course of social events no such regularity and invariance of phenomena as had already been found in the operation of human reasoning and in the sequence of natural phenomena. They did not search for the laws of social cooperation because they thought that man could organize society as he pleased. If social conditions did not fulfill the wishes of the reformers, if their utopias proved unrealizable, the fault was seen in the moral failure of man. Social problems were considered ethical problems. What was needed in order to construct the ideal society, they thought, were good princes and virtuous citizens. With righteous men any utopia might be realized.

The discovery of the inescapable interdependence of market phenomena overthrew this opinion. Bewildered, people had to face a new view of society. They learned with stupefaction that there is another aspect from which human action might be viewed than that of good and bad, of fair and unfair, of just and unjust. In the course of social events there prevails a regularity of phenomena to which man must adjust his actions if he wishes to succeed. It is futile to approach social facts with the attitude of a censor who approves or disapproves from the point of view of quite arbitrary standards and subjective judgments of value. One must study the laws of human action and social cooperation as the physicist studies the laws of nature. Human action and social cooperation seen as the object of a science of given relations, no longer as a normative discipline of things that ought to be--this was a revolution of tremendous consequences for knowledge and philosophy as well as for social action.

For more than a hundred years, however, the effects of this radical change in the methods of reasoning were greatly restricted because people believed that they referred only to a narrow segment of the total field of human action, namely, to market phenomena. The classical economists met in the pursuit of their investigations an obstacle which they failed to remove, the apparent antinomy of value. Their theory of value was defective, and forced them to restrict the scope [p. 3] of their science. Until the late nineteenth century political economy remained a science of the "economic" aspects of human action, a theory of wealth and selfishness. It dealt with human action only to the extent that it is actuated by what was --very unsatisfactorily--described as the profit motive, and it asserted that there is in addition other human action whose treatment is the task of other disciplines. The transformation of thought which the classical economists had initiated was brought to its consummation only by modern subjectivist economics, which converted the theory of market prices into a general theory of human choice.

For a long time men failed to realize that the transition from the classical theory of value to the subjective theory of value was much more than the substitution of a more satisfactory theory of market exchange for a less satisfactory one. The general theory of choice and preference goes far beyond the horizon which encompassed the scope of economic problems as circumscribed by the economists from Cantillon, Hume, and Adam Smith down to John Stuart Mill. It is much more than merely a theory of the "economic side" of human endeavors and of man's striving for commodities and an improvement in his material well-being. It is the science of every kind of human action. Choosing determines all human decisions. In making his choice man chooses not only between various material things and services. All human values are offered for option. All ends and all means, both material and ideal issues, the sublime and the base, the noble and the ignoble, are ranged in a single row and subjected to a decision which picks out one thing and sets aside another. Nothing that men aim at or want to avoid remains outside of this arrangement into a unique scale of gradation and preference. The modern theory of value widens the scientific horizon and enlarges the field of economic studies. Out of the political economy of the classical school emerges the general theory of human action, praxeology1. The economic or catallactic problems2 are embedded in a more general science, and can no longer be severed from this connection. No treatment of economic problems proper can avoid starting from acts of choice; economics becomes a part, although the hitherto best elaborated part, of a more universal science, praxeology. [p. 4]

  1. The term praxeology was first used in 1890 by Espinas. Cf. his article "Les Origines de law technologies," Revue Philosophique, XVth year, XXX, 114-115, and his book published in Paris in 1897, with the same title.
  2. The term Catallactics or the Science of Exchanges was first used by Whately. Cf. his book Introductory Lectures on Political Economy (London, 1831), p. 6.

Are we sure that we want to make Austrian Economics the "unofficial official economics" of /v/libertarian? I take issue with the idea that facts can be determined from priori knowledge instead of through empirical analysis and study. Hayek, Mises, Rothbard and others have expressed that praxeological statements can't be proved or disproved through testing.

“Praxeology is a theoretical and systematic, not a historical, science. Its scope is human action as such, irrespective of all environmental, accidental, and individual circumstances of the concrete acts. Its cognition is purely formal and general without reference to the material content and the particular features of the actual case. It aims at knowledge valid for all instances in which the conditions exactly correspond to those implied in its assumptions and inferences. Its statements and propositions are not derived from experience. They are, like those of logic and mathematics, a priori. They are not subject to verification or falsification on the ground of experience and facts.” - Human Action pg 32

I realize that Austrian econ lines up very nicely with Libertarian priors about political decentralization but this doesn't mean Libertarianism is incompatible with mainstream economics.

I have never seen someone make libertarianism compatible with mainstream economics, any links or arguments you would like to share? When you have the belief that government spending serves as a "multiplier" and is separate from individual spending I don't see how you can reconcile that with the belief in individual freedom. To me austrian economics and libertarianism are two sides of the same coin and I have yet to see a convincing argument otherwise.

This is my way of viewing it, though there's a good chance you'll disagree with me as you embrace libertarianism much more than I do. I'm about 60% libertarian and 40% utilitarian; with all my utilitarian coming from Economics as I don't find it useful to look at economics from a moral perspective. That'll probabaly be the deal breaker for you.

I first started with Austrian economics. I've read Economics in One Lesson and good amount of Man, Economy and State. Both of these books are pretty damning of government regulations in the market and of government failure in general. There were certainly some hard truths for me as I made a serious attempt at understanding of mainstream economics past the "Krugman must think hurricane sandy is stimulus" level. Through it I've eventually concluded that mainstream economics really isn't as hostile to Libertarian priors as I thought it was, we agree on a good amount, especially if you're Geo-libertarian. Many economists advocate:

  • Research seems to support the legalization of drugs and of black market goods and services in general like prostitution .

  • Land Value tax as it is the least distortionary tax. and has a whole host of benefits.

  • They advocate for a Carbon tax; a market solution to pollution which is the equivalent of making producers pay the cost of releasing carbon into the environment.

  • They advocate abolishing the Corporate income tax

  • They advocate weak immigration controls as they find it beneficial.

  • Replace Social Security with private Superannuation funds like in Australia.

  • They recognize that taxes on capital are not as efficient as they once thought and have devised alternatives to it in the face of Chamley-Judd; namely consumption taxes like the X tax.. Though their tune does change when it comes to Estate taxes, in the wake of PIkkety-Saez research the centrist view has become to levy an estate tax on large inheritances.

  • Oppose rent controls

  • Free trade is beneficial

All of these are roughly Libertarian ideals, stop the price controls, get the government out, stop the excessive taxation and let the market handle it, I think. Why aren't we implementing these polices instead of simply "when the economy goes into a recession we need stimulus"? Because politicians aren't interested in effective policy; they're interested in bailing out cronies and populist notions and then using a school of economics that vaguely justifies it. The state distorted Keynesian economics from "the government has a role in the economy during recessions and to correct market failures" to "lets regulate it all".

TL;DR the state ruined Keynesian economics and used it as an excuse to create a government monolith when this isn't necessarily what Keynesian economics advocates for.

If you'd like to ask about any specifics on Keynesian theory and how I reconcile it with roughly Libertarian ideals I'd be happy to answer. Call me on my bullshit if you see any :P

Read some David Friedman. The Machinery of Freedom is a good start. He's a libertarian anarcho-capitalist and a neoclassical economist. He also argues from an utilitarian perspective which I know a lot of libertarians really dislike but which is probably better at convincing a lot of people than arguments from natural law.

I have read both David and his Father and I think utilitarianism is a ridiculous way to justify a belief system. You wind up with the same kind of "needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few" BS that has plagued humanity for millennia. Then when you realize that it is ridiculous to justify a belief system a posteriori in a world where outcomes are never given in advance you wind up with some sort of rule utilitarianism which is just as absurd since you have no way of choosing who would create the rules without using the very system that you must create rules to achieve. It is just circular logic.

As a natural rights libertarian it is silly to me to advocate something that causes moral evil simply because it would work better, that is why I didn't really respond to the guy above. I find it impossible to talk with utilitarians because their point of view is just so radically different. The ends justifying the means is totally at odds with the belief in objective morality.
